idiom_name: state owner struct as supply half; render functions taking `&App`/`&ViewModel` as the presentational half (Leptos signals as the framework route)
implementation_notes: Rust's standard library has no component runtime and no re-render step, so the honest realization is the hand-written split: one struct owns the data and its source, and presentation happens in functions that take that state by reference and return markup or paint into a buffer - `fn render(app: &App, frame: &mut Frame)` - with no state inside the widgets. Ownership encodes the rule: the supply half mutates, the render half borrows immutably, and a widget that wants to keep its own copy has to fight the borrow checker to get one. Where a reactive web UI is wanted, Leptos is the documented alternative - a component is a setup function returning a view, props are plain struct fields and signals carry the data. The hand-written form stays justified for terminal UIs (ratatui's immediate mode redraws every frame from the current data, which is exactly this shape) and for embeddable engines.
pitfalls: Widgets that cache their own copy of the data (Rc<RefCell<..>> next to the widget, self-referential structs) undermine the single owner; keep the dependency direction owner to renderer.
Splitting state across several owners forces interior mutability (Rc<RefCell<..>>, Arc<Mutex<..>>) and reintroduces the aliasing bugs the single owner avoided.
Redrawing every frame is intentional in immediate mode; cloning large collections every frame is not - borrow, or pass iterators.
